name: Smoky Black
lede: Smoky Black is a near-black with a faint warm cast, close enough to true black that our own library flags it as an obscure, qualified name rather than a mainstream one.

sections.title: Barely a color apart from black
sections.body:
ColorHub's library records Smoky Black with a usage rank near the bottom of its list and tags it directly as "obscure, qualified or novelty" [1]. By ISCC-NBS classification it reads as a brownish black, only 3.6 units from its nearest block and 4.8 units from plain [[black]] itself, which is a small enough gap that most eyes would not separate the two without a side-by-side swatch [2]. Who coined "smoky black" and when is not recorded in the sources we checked, so its origin stays undocumented here [1]. Our library also cross-references the Japanese name *Kokushoku* (黒色), meaning simply "black," as an equivalent rather than a source for the English name [1].

The word "smoky" is doing real descriptive work even at this extreme: real smoke rising against a dark background reads with exactly this kind of warm, slightly brown-grey cast rather than pure neutral black, the same quality separating [[charcoal]] from [[ebony]].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds a close match to Smoky Black in 6,180 of 23,781 paintings, nearly 26 percent, with the within-painting test still finding 5,487, making it more common than every other named color we track [3]. It peaks in the 1600s, in 1948 of 6,394 paintings, the century of deep Baroque shadow painting, present in over 30 percent of our paintings from then [3]. The painter most devoted to it, relative to his peers, is Nicolaes Maes, carrying it in 18 of 21 works in the archive, about 2.9 times the rate of the museums his paintings come from [3]. Inside the paintings that carry it, the color plays a shadow 68 percent of the time, exactly what its name and its ubiquity in dark Baroque backgrounds would predict [3]. All counts are matches in photographs of aged, varnished canvases, not pigment identifications [3]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, read as screen colors, not pigment identifications[3].
